claims.text: Annealing Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni at 800–900°C for 1–4 hours can increase or otherwise systematically modify its short-range order.
An optimal, moderate level of short-range order kinetically slows phase decomposition.
The optimal short-range-order level arises from a balance between mixed-valence-driven enthalpic attractions and configurational entropy.
Mixed-valence interactions induce local atomic clustering or ordering in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni.
Configurational entropy competes with mixed-valence-driven local ordering in this alloy.
Moderate short-range order creates a kinetic barrier to phase separation.
Moderate short-range order suppresses unwanted precipitate formation.
Too little short-range order provides insufficient microstructural stabilization.
Excessive short-range order promotes over-nucleation of secondary phases.
Secondary-phase formation caused by excessive short-range order degrades the targeted property combination.
Optimally enhanced short-range order will retain higher high-temperature strength than the baseline treatment.
Optimally enhanced short-range order will improve environmental resistance relative to the baseline.
Optimally enhanced short-range order will improve radiation tolerance relative to the baseline.
Optimally enhanced short-range order will maintain cryogenic toughness relative to the baseline.
The baseline treatment of 600°C for 2 hours produces a default or standard short-range-order level.
Diffraction peak shifts and intensity changes can serve as indicators of changes in short-range order.
Atom-probe tomography can quantify local clustering associated with short-range order.
Annealing at approximately 850°C for 2 hours will produce a moderate short-range-order condition.
Annealing at approximately 900°C for 4 hours will produce an excessively ordered condition with secondary-phase precipitation.
The proposed mechanism is limited to inert annealing between 600°C and 900°C for holding times of 1–4 hours and may not apply after composition changes.
